        About:

        Can that sign actually get you towed?

        I checked every temporary tow-away permit San Francisco Public Works has published, plus the posted hours the city lists for each street segment, so you don’t have to. Unofficial, not affiliated with SFMTA or SF Public Works.

        Created by Andrew Baker. Inspired by Greg Long’s post on SF street space permits.

        About this data and the counts

        Tow Status comes straight from the public permit record as of the last snapshot. It isn’t live enforcement data. Picking another date changes which permits are shown, not their status.

        The map starts with Not Enforceable permits covering today. The city record says these can’t be used to tow, so their curbs are often open. Enforceable permits outside their listed hours are left out, since other drivers can read those signs too. Street cleaning, meters, time limits and other posted rules still apply.

        Dates are the inclusive tow-away start and end dates, falling back to permit dates, then expiration. Permits with missing or invalid dates appear only under All dates. Permit details list the city’s posted hours for each street segment.

        Locations come from exact address matches to the city’s Enterprise Addressing System, so a dot marks an address, not the exact curb. Permits at the same address share one dot. Permits without a match are included in whole-city lists and counts, but not on the map or in map-view results.

        Your location is only used in your browser to center the map; this site doesn’t store or send it. After you use “Show spots near me,” this device remembers to find you on later visits. You can turn that off in the footer.

        Public Works’ street space guidance explains how tow signs become enforceable. Always check the posted sign. Spot a problem? Let me know on X.
